import subprocess
import threading

argv = ["pacman", "-S", "r22-threadruninline"]

def worker(argv):
    subprocess.run(argv)

threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(argv,)).run()
rationale: The chained expression threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(argv,)).run() never starts a thread: attribute .run resolves to Thread.run on the fresh instance, which is an ordinary synchronous method call in the caller. Per CPython 3.14.8 threading.Thread.__init__ (Lib/threading.py, source snapshot lines 925-928), target=worker binds self._target = worker and args=(argv,) binds self._args = (argv,); run() (lines 1013-1028) then executes self._target(*self._args, **self._kwargs), i.e. worker(argv), in this same frame. argv is a literal module-level list ["pacman", "-S", "r22-threadruninline"], so worker's parameter binds to that exact vector and subprocess.run receives exactly the command 'pacman -S r22-threadruninline'. A pacman -S install transaction is a host mutation; every link in the call chain (constructor keywords, run dispatch, argv binding) is statically resolvable, so the row is observed, not a lead, and there is nothing unparsed. The transient Thread object being unbound to any name does not change semantics: .run() runs before the object is discarded.
